**The Library of Babel** – A short story describing an infinite library of hexagonal rooms that contains every possible 410‑page book, a hallmark image of Borges’ fascination with endless combinatorial spaces.  

**Ficciones** – Borges’ most famous 1944 collection, which brings together many of his signature stories such as “The Library of Babel,” “The Garden of Forking Paths,” and “The Aleph.”  

**The Aleph** – A story in which the protagonist discovers a point in a basement that shows every place in the universe simultaneously, illustrating Borges’ preoccupation with total knowledge.  

**The Garden of Forking Paths** – The title story of the same‑named collection, featuring the Chinese spy Yu Tsun and a novel that branches into infinite alternative histories.  

**Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote** – A fictional literary criticism in which Menard attempts to recreate Cervantes’ *Don Quixote* word for word, exemplifying Borges’s meta‑fictional playfulness.  

**Yu Tsun** – The German spy protagonist of “The Garden of Forking Paths” who murders the sinologist Stephen Albert to transmit a secret location, a recurring character in Borges’s espionage‑themed tales.  

**Hexagonal rooms / infinite library** – The architectural motif of endless, interconnected hexagonal chambers that house every possible book, central to “The Library of Babel” and other Borges stories.  

**The Purifiers** – A fanatical group that roams the infinite library, destroying books they deem nonsense; they appear in several Borges narratives set in the hexagonal library.  

**Ts’ui Pen** – The legendary Chinese author whose unfinished novel is described as a labyrinth containing all possible futures; his work is referenced in “The Garden of Forking Paths.”  

**Sinologist Stephen Albert** – The scholar killed by Yu Tsun in “The Garden of Forking Paths,” whose knowledge of Ts’ui Pen’s labyrinth triggers the story’s climax.  

**Death and the Compass** – A detective story where the investigator Lonnrot is lured into a trap by Red Scharlach using a Tetragrammaton puzzle, showcasing Borges’s blend of mystery and philosophy.  

**The Sect of the Phoenix** – A short story about an obscure cult that lacks a common memory, reflecting Borges’s interest in secret societies and the fluidity of identity.  

**The South (El Sur)** – A tale in which the protagonist Juan Dahlmann meets a fatal knife duel in a rural Argentine setting, often cited as a quintessential Borges narrative of fate and honor.  

**The Book of Sand** – A story about an infinite book with no beginning or end, symbolizing the endlessness of textual possibilities and Borges’s obsession with the boundless nature of literature.
